ety.text: Proto-Indo-European *pṓdsder. Ancient Greek πούς (poús) Ancient Greek ὀκτώπους (oktṓpous)bor. Latin octōpūsbor. English octopus Borrowed from Latin octōpūs, from Ancient Greek ὀκτώπους (oktṓpous), from ὀκτώ (oktṓ, “eight”) + πούς (poús, “foot”). Piecewise doublet of octopod and octopede.

senses.d: Any of several marine molluscs of the order Octopoda, having no internal or external protective shell or bone (unlike the nautilus, squid and cuttlefish) and eight arms each covered with suckers.
ex: Even octopuses without stylets almost certainly retain the molecular machinery necessary to build them.

senses.d: The flesh of these marine molluscs eaten as food.
An organization that has many powerful branches controlled from the centre.
An instance of a player scoring a touchdown immediately followed by a successful two-point conversion, resulting in a total score of eight points.
A safety device allowing divers to share an air supply in an emergency.
To put (or attempt to put) one's fingers, hands or arms in many things or places at roughly the same time.
ex: He rises up on his wasted legs, the healer's hands octopussed on his head.
I took off my shirt, standing in swim trunks, embarrassed of my tour body, my hands octopussing around the ashamed drink tickets of my gut.

senses.d: To spread out in long arms or legs in many directions.
ex: The bug-eyed press octopussed to their respective word processors.
Dirt roads octopussed into the interior, where there were more dried mud and shrivelled crops.

senses.d: To plug a large number of devices into a single electric outlet.
ex: By now, the reservation had electricity so THAT had to be octopussed out to the trailers too.
It was an eight-channel audio recording snake, a bundled set of cables with eight plugs octopussing out of either end.

senses.d: To grow in use vastly beyond what was originally intended.
ex: The performance of it, however, did not improve, being octopussed by centuries-old not-to-move bureaucracy.
The sport could be called octopusing or octopus hunting— and any number may play. Supposing you catch an octopus, what do you have?
CRABBING AND OCTOPUSSING: Use the same method whether you skindive for crabs and octopi or gather them intertidally.
Night fell especially dark and cold for August, inky blackness tendrilling in, octopussing even the street lamps, now dim with vague form.

ety.text: From Guernsey Norman pieuvre (introduced or popularised by Victor Hugo ca. 1866; cf. also Old Northern French puerve). Ultimately from Latin polypūs (via *pueleve, *puelve, *pueuve, *pieuve, with the same /w/ > /j/ dissimilation as in yeux), from Ancient Greek πολύπους (polúpous, “several feet”). Doublet of poulpe.
Ultimately borrowed from Latin polypūs, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek πολύπους (polúpous). Doublet of polype and pieuvre.
From Latin polypus, from Ancient Greek πολύπους (polúpous). Cognates include Spanish pulpo and Sicilian purpu. Unrelated to polpa.
Borrowed from French pieuvre, ultimately from Latin polypus, Ancient Greek πολύπους (polúpous).

it:ottopode.gl: octopus (any mollusk of the family Octopodidae)

ety.text: Inherited from Latin polypus (“cuttlefish, polyp”) (compare Catalan polp, pop, French poulpe, Galician polbo, Italian polpo, Portuguese polvo), from a variant of Ancient Greek πολύπους (polúpous, literally “many footed”), from πολύς (polús, “many”) + πούς (poús, “foot”). Doublet of pólipo.

From Old Galician-Portuguese polbo, from Latin polypus (“octopus”), from Ancient Greek πολύπους (polúpous). Doublet of pólipo. Cognate with Galician polbo, Spanish pulpo, Italian polpo, French poulpe, pieuvre.
